utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Hasan Younis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the appearances for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now resume after the weekend break. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. We have a witness scheduled for today. But before we hear this witness, we would like to clarify the issue of broadcasting videotape. The Trial Chamber has deliberated on the matter and we believe that as of Wednesday, we should broadcast as a matter of priority the videotapes for which we already have a transcript available. So the videotapes that have transcripts are concerned [as interpreted], and these videos should be broadcast, should be shown, as a matter of priority. The Prosecution should then provide us a transcript of the videos for which there are no official transcripts for the moment. They should do so in good time. This might pose a technical problem for the Prosecution, but if that is the case it would be sufficient for the Prosecution to view the videotape themselves and then they could use someone to take down what is said in the video to form a transcript. This could then be provided to the Judges before the video or the videos are broadcast. This is how we would like these videos to be broadcast. This is a procedure we would like to follow. Mr. Mundis, do you see any difficulties in proceeding in this matter? Do you see any difficulties that might arise as a result of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could briefly consult with my colleague, Mr. Neuner, who is present here in the courtroom. He has actually been responsible for the videotapes. If I could just have a moment to consult with him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Chamber's order clarifying the previous order with respect to the videotapes does not seem to pose a problem as we're sitting here in court today. It appears as though the videos which we have selected for viewing tomorrow do, in fact, have transcripts. We are -- as we speak, our team members are in the process of ensuring that there are sufficient photocopies of the transcripts for everyone in and around the courtroom, including the interpretation booths. Because of the large number of transcripts and the fact that we need to produce 11 sets of them, we may not have that available by close of business today. We will, of course, endeavour to ensure that everyone has a copy of the transcripts first thing in the morning tomorrow to the extent that we have transcripts. I should also point out, Mr. President, that there are a few of the videos which do not have anyone really audibly speaking on them. So there aren't obviously transcripts for those. If I could -- also just to inform the Chamber and the Defence, we are -- we will provide in effect a spreadsheet indicating which tapes and which segments of those tapes we're planning on broadcasting. As of right now, we have 189 minutes - that's a little bit more than three hours - prepared for viewing tomorrow. That comes -- that material comes from a number of the videotapes. And as I indicated last Friday, those are for the most part excerpts and selected portions of tapes, although a couple of the tapes will be played -- four of the tapes will be shown in their entirety as part of that three hours and a few moments of tape that we have scheduled for tomorrow. We will, of course, be in a position tomorrow to address tapes to be shown Thursday and Friday if the Trial Chamber in fact does want to view tapes for all three days after today of this week. But I don't believe it's a problem, Mr. President, with respect to the transcripts. Although again, it might not physically be in everyone's hands by close of business today. We are, in fact, working on that, and Mr. Neuner will actually be with your leave departing the courtroom in a few moments in order to oversee that project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Mundis. The Trial Chamber thanks you for your response. You've addressed the main concern, and that was to have transcripts for these videos. Naturally, if there is nothing audible on certain videos, there won't be any transcripts; that's obvious. You said you have prepared four videos for tomorrow, and you will be able to provide everyone, the Judges included, with transcripts of these videotapes. Is there anything that the Defence would like to say? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Madam Judge; good day, Your Honours. Mr. President, at this point in time, the Defence would like certain clarifications regarding the procedure we will be following when viewing the videos. In the past, we have already expressed our position, and we have stated that if we have no information on how a video was produced, if we don't know who made the video, if we don't know who compiled the video, who made a sort of collage, if we don't know who may have written the text that appears, if we don't know who's speaking on the video, if we know nothing about the images on the video, if we don't when they were taken, if we don't know in which year, if we don't know where the video was made, in our opinion the Defence believes that he should have a minimum of information before we view such videos. We don't want to be carried away by viewing a video that might seem very interesting, but has no reliability whatsoever. Mr. President, when the Trial Chamber rendered its decision on viewing these videos, it was our understanding that the Trial Chamber was requesting that the Prosecution present a witness who would appear at least to authenticate the video. But as things stand, Mr. President, we have no information to that effect. We believe it would be premature to start viewing these videos without having the minimum information that we require. I don't have all the legal arguments at hand, Mr. President, but tomorrow morning I could present the Defence's arguments for one final time with regard to this matter because in our opinion it's a very important matter. It doesn't concern the contents of the video; it concerns the reliability of the video. We're concerned that all decisions taken by the Chamber should be taken on the basis of evidence that has minimum reliability and whose contents have minimum reliability. In this case, Mr. President, it is our opinion that if we have no witness to authenticate the video, this cast doubts on the reliability. We need someone to appear before the Court in order to provide this information and any additional information that might support the evidence that has already been admitted. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In summary, Mr. President, the Defence would like some clarifications from the Trial Chamber. Does the Trial Chamber believe that a video can be admitted into evidence if we have no information as to the source of the video, as to how it was made, or if we have no information about the contents? We would like to know where the contents come from and what it's supposed to represent. We would simply like to know whether the Trial Chamber believes such evidence could be admitted. If you do believe that it can be admitted into evidence, we're prepared to view the video. But in our opinion, the law does not permit such video material to be admitted into evidence if we don't have a minimum of information. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Just one additional point, and that is if I could my learned friend from the Prosecution whether the spreadsheet from the videos could be available today before the end of Court so we're able to view that this evening and prepare. Because our one request at the very least tomorrow would be that we are able to respond to any of the videos that are shown and present arguments as to why those particular videos should or should not be admissible as evidence in the case. It would assist greatly if we could have that information before the close of court today. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon, with regard to what you have said -- I'll now let Mr. Mundis take the floor again. The Trial Chamber spent hours deliberating on the matter of videos. Our decision was quite clear. We said that these videos would be viewed, and that after viewing them the Trial Chamber would reach a final decision on the admissibility into evidence, on the admissibility of these videos. The Trial Chamber also said that having viewed the videos, if it seemed necessary to call a witness, we would naturally reserve the right to call such a witness, a witness who could come to authenticate the video. As you know, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence state that when the Prosecution compiles a list of witnesses and exhibits, the Defence, who has a list of exhibits, should at that point in time state or make any legal comments it has about the documentary evidence listed. When this list is compiled -- when the list was compiled, the Defence didn't make any legal comments. I reminded you of this a few days ago. You made some legal comments a few days ago. We took note of it. On page 4, line 19 and after -- and onwards, there was a series of questions put. I believe that the Prosecution, before the video is broadcast, will provide all the necessary information about the date when the video was made, about the author of the video, about the manner in which they managed to obtain the video, and about whom they obtained it from. So they will answer the questions that you put on page 4 from line 19 onwards. The Trial Chamber mentioned how we would proceed before the video was broadcast. The Prosecution can address your issues, the issues that I have referred to, and then everyone will view the video. At that point in time, the Defence will be able to take the floor to repeat what they have just said, what you have just said, if necessary. And then the Trial Chamber will deliberate in light of the comments of both parties. So roughly speaking, this is the procedure we have decided to follow. We made this decision a long time ago. Mr. Mundis, in light of what has been said, is there anything you would like to say? You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do, in fact, have the spreadsheet to which I referred earlier. And if the usher could assist, perhaps this could be distributed right now, and I can make a few explanatory comments for the benefits of the Chamber and the Defence. While that's being done, Mr. President, with respect to the comments that Your Honour just made, of course the Prosecution will be in a position to provide the full details with respect to each segment of the videotape, of course, to the extent we have all of that information. We will certainly provide the Chamber and the Defence with specific information concerning each excerpt or full tape that's broadcast immediately prior to that segment or tape being broadcast. I will inform the Chamber and Defence that we do not have all the specific details about each and every tape; however, that information which is in our possession, we will, of course, describe prior to showing the tape. If I could turn very quickly to the spreadsheet which has been distributed. The first column under "order" sets forth the categories, if you will, for which these tapes are relevant. The ERN number sets forth, obviously, the number of the tape. The third column describes the length of the entire tape. And the fourth column indicates the amount of time, or the excerpt if it's a lengthy tape, which will be broadcast. So, for example, the first tape listed is a total of 4 minutes and we will play that entire tape. The second tape runs for 1 hour, 14 minutes. We will play a 6-minute excerpt with the times indicated so that the Defence has the opportunity to review the 6 minutes that we are proposing to show from that tape, et cetera. You'll see that we've -- when we have excerpted material from lengthy tapes, the precise timings where those excerpts can be found on the original tapes is indicated on the spreadsheet. And again, if you total up the bold numbers in the fourth column, that will get you to the figure of 189 minutes which is slightly longer than three hours. You'll note, Mr. President, that in effect there are 11 sequences set forth. These 11 sequences come from six videotapes -- excuse me, eight videotapes. We are planning of shows four of those tapes in total, and four of those tapes we are showing excerpts from, a total of seven excerpts from those four videotapes. And that is really what the spreadsheet indicates, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence has the spreadsheet containing all the information that has been mentioned. The Defence has understood that there are videotapes which won't be broadcast in their entirety. The Prosecution will select certain excerpts to be broadcast. But as the Defence has seen the videos, I assume that if the Defence believes that the excerpts don't represent the truth contained in the videos, in such a case the Defence can request that such sections be shown. You've already seen these videos, whereas the Judges haven't. But as the Defence has already seen the videos, if you believe you should draw the attention of the Judges to a certain section, you should inform us of the fact. We'll then see or view the entire tape. This spreadsheet will enable us to find our bearings. Mr. Mundis has said that before a video is broadcast, he will address the concerns that you raised with regard to the reliability of the material. If you encounter any difficulties while we are following this procedure, you will inform us of the problem, and the Judges will decide on the action to be taken. We will now call the witness into the courtroom. Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could while the witness is being brought into the courtroom, address Your Honours with respect to one issue concerning this witness. During the proofing session of this witness earlier this morning, he indicated that the level of detail that's contained in his written statement, it is very difficult for him to recall with a high degree of specificity. The witness, Mr. President, is a relatively young 67 years of age and of course is testifying about events 11 years ago. I spoke with the Defence prior to this afternoon's session. It was my intention to tender the witness's written statement pursuant to Rule 89 (D) and then to allow him to be cross-examined by the Defence. The Defence proposed another course of action, primarily because the witness has a diary, if you will, of the events in question. The Defence have proposed that the witness be permitted to consult his diary during his direct examination. I also explained to them that I may at times be required to lead the evidence of this witness, and the Defence indicated that they would not necessarily object to that procedure being used. I simply indicate this, Mr. President, because if I have to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. refresh the witness's recollection by taking him to his written witness statement, his direct examination will be substantially longer than would be the case, obviously, if I were permitted to lead him and he were permitted to refer to his diary. Of course, the other alternative would be we would lay the foundation and then seek to tender his written statement pursuant to Rule 89 (D), and then he would be cross-examined by the Defence and questioned by Your Honours. I simply raise this because again I anticipate that when this witness was selected, it was partially due to the high level of specifics in his statement, many of which he is not in a position at this time to recall with a high degree of specificity. I leave it to Your Honours in terms of which of those two options might be most useful for the Trial Chamber. I clearly do not have a copy of his written witness statement in French, so that may or may not have a bearing on a decision. But we are prepared to pursue either of these two courses of action in order to keep the direct examination to a bare minimum in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will give the floor to the Defence now. But according to what we have understood, you are saying that this witness who is relative young as he is 67 years old, no longer remembers certain facts very accurately, certain events that took place over 10 years ago. And as a result, he has his diary with him. By consulting this diary, it would be easier for him to answer the questions put to him. In addition, you are suggesting that in order to refresh the witness's memory, you would be grateful if you were given leave to ask him more precise questions. You say that you have consulted the Defence about this matter, and the Defence has agreed or has reached an agreement with you as to how you should proceed. Naturally, the Trial Chamber is always in favour of the parties reaching an agreement, and we'll try to see what the situation is by asking the Defence to state what its position is. Mr. Bourgon, or Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In fact we did confer with our colleague from the Prosecution a little earlier on. And we have also been able to meet the witness and to speak to him very briefly. And we realised that perhaps there might be certain difficulties as far as the witness's memory is concerned. And for this reason, and in the interests of justice, Mr. President, we would agree with the Prosecution that they should be allowed to refresh the witness's memory and that the witness should be allowed to use his notes. We also agree that the Prosecution could lead the witness to a certain extent in order to be able to proceed as rapidly as possible. And Mr. President, this would also enable us to cross-examine the witness and take less time doing so than if we cross-examined the witness pursuant to Rule 189 [as interpreted] -- or rather, it would be more rapid than tendering the witness's statement into evidence pursuant to this rule. We think it would be good if we could have a copy of the witness's notes. We don't know if his notes in Swedish or in English. If the witness's notes in Swedish, we'll proceed without his notes. But if his notes are in English, having a copy would enable us to proceed more rapidly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We had spoken to the Prosecution before about this matter. In order to speed up proceedings, there's no objection on our part, if the witness does require his notes that he be entitled to refer to them. It might be that he doesn't need them for many issues, certainly issues of a more general nature. But if there are to be specific questions and he can't remember through the questions being put, then there's no objection to him looking at his diary or his notebook. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one matter I'd like to address: As far as the written statement is concerned, if we accepted the solution that has been suggested, if we agree to have the witness consult his notes and if these notes are in English, we could show the notes to the Defence, it would then not be necessary to tender the written statement into evidence. Mr. Mundis, is this what you are suggesting that we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It would be an either/or. We would not obviously seek to tender the witness's written statement in the event he were to testify primarily orally, even though he may on occasion have to refer to his notebook. We would in that case not be seeking to tender his written statement pursuant to Rule 89 (D). We would only do that if we weren't allowed to lead the witness occasionally and to allow him to refer to his diary for his direct examination. Let me also very briefly mention two other things: First of all, the Prosecution does not have the witness's diary, nor did we make a copy of that at any point in time. I am not sure if the witness's diary is in English or Swedish. I'm also assuming that if he is to be allowed to use his diary, we should inform Madam Usher because my guess is he probably left it in the waiting room and may not bring the diary into the courtroom because I specifically advised him that he was not allowed to use his diary unless, of course, Your Honours permitted that. So he might not actually have it in his hands. I assume he did bring it with him, though, to the witness waiting room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is how we will proceed. If necessary, we will ask the witness to fetch his notebook. We will then see whether his notes are in Swedish or in English. If the diary is in English, then if the witness agrees we will show the notes to both parties and then we will start with the examination of the witness. Very well, let's call the witness into the courtroom now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understood, but maybe I'm wrong, but you would also like to use his written statement in order to refresh his memory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not actually planning on doing that unless it's absolutely clear that his diary is of no assistance. The witness explained to me this morning when I met with him how his statement was written up when he met with the investigator. They actually sat down together with the witness's diary and used, took many parts of the diary, particularly the dates and information for specific dates, and incorporated that into his written statement. So my understanding from discussing it with the witness is actually that the diary formed the basis for the written witness statement. So if he has got his diary, I don't think he would need to be referred to his written statement. But if there were gaps, then again, I may need to refresh his memory based on the information contained in his written witness statement which, of course, the Defence has copies of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom now. But could you tell him to come with his notebook. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have four documents to tender with regard to the other witness, Martin Garrod. I don't know if you would want me to do this straightaway or after this next witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll do it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'd just like to check that you can hear everyone, the interpretation. And if you are able to hear, please say yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called by the Prosecution as witness, and in the coming minutes you're going to be asked to take the solemn declaration. Before you take the solemn Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. declaration, I would like you to identify yourself. So could you please give us your name and surname, your date of birth, place of birth, and nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My nationality is Swedish. And I was born the 2nd of August 1937. My name is Torbjorn Junhov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession or what post do you occupy? What is your job at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At present I am a pensioner, retired from the military service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You have completed your professional military career with what rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what function did you occupy in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started as a monitor attached to the original -- what do you call it? In Zenica. I started as a team member, and then I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Have you already testified before a national tribunal or an international tribunal or is this the first time that you are giving testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was here in 1998. And that's the only case I have been in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the case you testified in? And were you a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness. And the case was allegation against the commander or the chief of the prison in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now ask you to take the solemn declaration. Read from the card that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I should like to give you some information with respect to the proceedings here this afternoon and your testimony. You are going to first be answering questions put to you by the representative of the Prosecution in the person of Mr. Mundis, who is sitting to your right. And once he has completed his questions, you will be asked to respond. And once he has completed all his questions, the Defence counsel will be asking you questions, too. And they are sitting to your left. I think that you have already met them while preparing today's testimony or taking part in the courtroom here. Once you have heard questions from both parties, the Judges might wish you to ask you additional questions. And the Judges, as I say, can also ask. So after the Defence has asked questions, the Prosecution has the right to redirect, and then the Judges might wish to ask you questions. But I should like to ask you to make pauses between question and answer, and then they will be a pause before the Judges ask their questions, if they need to do so. You have taken the solemn declaration to speak the truth, which of course excludes all false testimony. I should just like to remind the witness, as this is my job, that this -- should you not speak the truth, then this will entail sanctions by the Tribunal. And there is another ruling - but this does not apply to you - that a witness can always refuse to answer a question if they consider that their answer might be incriminating. In that case, the Chamber can ask the witness to answer the question nonetheless, but that they guarantee him immunity for the testimony he gives. The Prosecution has informed the Chamber that the facts that you're going to testify about span a period of 10 years, and that of course you might have forgotten certain details that are contained in your written statement. The Prosecution has informed the Chamber that you have in your possession a diary tracing, if I can put it that way, the events as they came to pass, the events that you wrote down in that diary. Now, we can see that you have something beside you and we would like to ask you whether that notebook is in Swedish or in English? The entries, are they in Swedish or in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mixed. Very well. Now, could you take the diary out of the case it's in. Is it a lengthy book? How many pages, would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have -- the diary is day-by-day notes from my arrival in the beginning of April and ends up on the 21st of June. And I also have another notebook, what I call the "black book" with notes from the same period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the black book, is that in English, Swedish, or mixed again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's also mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mind if you give us those books for a moment so that the Prosecution and Defence counsels can take a look at them, at the black-book notebook and the diary, to facilitate with the questioning? Would you have anything against having Madam Usher take the two notebooks to show them to the Prosecution and the Defence counsel before we start the examination-in-chief? And of course, if you need to do so later on, then you'll be able to consult them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have nothing against that. But I would like to inform you that during the investigations that lasted for I think two or three days, the investigator from the Tribunal together with me, we went through all these notes and all these notes are included in my written testimony. Not all, but the most essential of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the procedure is such that it is purely oral. So the written statement was not a priori given to witnesses for the purpose of them answering the questions posed; in theory, the witness is expected to answer questions without looking at any document, including his written statement. Now, of course, in particular cases such as your own, you do have in your possession these two notebooks which will assist you in finding your way in responding to the questions. So the Defence wish to have a look at those documents. Now, do you have anything against us showing the Defence counsel the black-book notebook and the other one, and they will hand it back to you immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Usher, would you please take the two documents and show them to the counsel. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The procedure has not been perhaps explained as clearly as possible. Perhaps we could have a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we need to photocopy this, we'll have to adjourn, and that will take a long time. At least an hour. So you can take your time to have a look at the two documents as they're handed to you. Of course, everything that is in Swedish, you won't be able to understand. But...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as the witness has just said, he is ready and willing to assist. Mr. Junhov, your two notebooks, how many pages would you say in total in them? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's three months, and notes for almost every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how many pages would you say? 50? 100? 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 150, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 150 pages, you say. Because there is yet another solution and that is to photocopy them. But then, of course, the photocopy would mean that you agree to the existence of a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see no obstacle or hinder for that. It's a question of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that if we look at the three months, there are two pages for one day, at least 100 pages. So if we had them, this would be very useful. And of course, the witness could keep the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best course would be to make a photo -- make photocopies of them, which would mean an adjournment of 15 minutes. And we're going to ask the Registrar to help us out, to have four photocopies made, one for the Prosecution, one set for the -- or rather, two sets for the two Defence teams, and one set of photocopies for the Chamber, for the Judges. So we're going to adjourn for 15 minutes, which will give us enough time to photocopy the notebooks, and we will reconvene in 15 minutes' time. --- Break taken at 3.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to give the notebooks back to the witness now, these documents, along with the photocopy. The Chamber doesn't need the photocopy at present. So now I hope that everybody has received a set of photocopies which will allow the parties to put their questions. And having said that, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis without further ado, and of course we have set the frameworks for the general questioning and examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Mundis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Junhov.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us in response to one of the preliminary question by the Trial Chamber you had a career in the military. Can you tell us, please, which branch of the Swedish military you served in.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I started at 19 years old in 1956. I volunteered for the Swedish Air Force and got training as a navigator. And after a number of years in flying service, I was appointed to the schools and took my officer degree in 1964. And after that, I served in different units up until 1968 when I went to the War and Staff College for three years' studies. And during the 1970s, I served in the Swedish military headquarters dealing with studies in long-term planning, cooperation with the civilian defence and these kind of questions. Then I had a period of service in a unit, and also in a regional staff as an operational officer. And for four years in the second part of the 1980s I was a professor at the Staff and War College. And I was a professor responsible for strategy, security policy, military history, and human rights. And then again some years of service in the regional military staff as head of the operational part of the staff; and then back to the military academy as a professor where we trained mostly civilian officers within the Swedish organisation that is called the total defence. That has very much to do with nongovernmental organisation, cooperation in wartime, and how to cope with the different problems that occurs in the wartime. And then after that session, I was back again in the regional staff up until the spring 1993 when I was asked by the military headquarters if I could go as a civilian monitor to the ECMM operation in former Yugoslavia. So I agreed to that and served there for three months. And then when I came back, I have been occupied mostly with teaching people from the Baltic states within the framework of the Partnership For Peace agreement with Swedish authorities and our neighbours. And then I retired 1997. And now I'm running a company dealing with -- I am an editor, local history books and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, I'd like to focus your attention now on the period of time when you were an ECMM monitor. Can you tell us what kind of specialised briefings or training that you had prior to your deployment as an ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Shortly after I was appointed as a monitor, we were called up. We were a group of, if I remember, eight Swedish officers who were planning to go to former Yugoslavia. We had two or three days' briefings in Stockholm on the situation in general in the Balkans was presented and discussed. And we also had got some equipment and so on. And we had diplomatic passports. We were unarmed and all dressed in white clothes. And then we went down to the headquarters in Zagreb, Hotel I, where the ECMM headquarters occupied the whole hotel. And during three or four days staying there, we were briefed on rules of operation and how to handle communication equipment and how to drive the cars. And then I was appointed as a monitor to Zenica. And that was first time in my life I heard the word "Zenica." They took us by a very, very rough journey down to Split and stayed with a couple of days with a logistics base for the ECMM in Split. And then we had, I think, five failed attempts to take us into Central Bosnia. It was wintertime and totally blocked roads, either with snow or by military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us the approximate date, including the month and year, that you arrived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I think it was -- it was in -- I left home in the Easter days, 1993. And if I remember correct, I arrived in Zagreb 25th, 26th of March. And then I think my first day in Zenica was 31st of May -- or March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Zenica? Or perhaps the other way to phrase it is: When did you leave Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I left -- I had one week holiday, the first week of June. And then I left definitely the 21st of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than this one-week holiday in the first week of June 1993, did you remain in Zenica for that entire period?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes. Zenica or in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about your specific duties and responsibilities as an EC monitor in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to start with my first impressions when we came across the mountains from Split into Central Bosnia and I saw all these damaged houses and empty houses, no sign of life. And I started to think "what has happened to these people?" And thinking of Geneva Conventions and human rights and how to behave in the war and so on. And when I reported for the first time to the head of the -- our CC, the French diplomat, Jean-Pierre Thebault, we had dinner together, sat up talking almost the whole night, the first night I was there and he explained to me what the situation looked like in Central Bosnia. And I, of course, didn't understand immediately that it was a civil war and a lot of warring parties engaged in this war. Quite soon, I think it was the second or the third day of my being there, I was appointed as a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission. The war had started in Busovaca, as I explained. And the ECMM had an intention to reunify the Busovaca Municipality. We have a lot of meetings there. And after some weeks, I was appointed as a chairman of this commission. And then we also established similar commissions in Vitez and in Travnik. I was engaged in that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The first intention was to reunify the split municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could tell us, you've mentioned the Busovaca, Vitez, and Travnik commissions. How many commissions in total were operating during the period you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: It's hard to say because some of them were just intentions. They never started. We also had an ambition to create a joint operational command in Travnik. And that was in the beginning of June 1993 with the HVO and the BiH officers, and a joint command post in the PTT building in Travnik. But that joint command in practice never worked, mostly due to lack of communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll return later to the joint command in Travnik. I'd like to ask you a few questions about the Busovaca commission. I take it from your answer that that is the commission that you were the most familiar with.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the representatives of the various parties or groups that attended the meetings at the Busovaca commission?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I don't remember the names of the local persons. There was an HVO battalion commander with a command post in central Busovaca. I don't remember his name. There were different so-called local commanders. I regarded them as some kind of elderly people from the villages around in the municipality. And from the military side, there was -- the HVO representative was Mr. Nakic and from the BiH, it was Mr. Merdan. And these two were, as I understood, second in command in their representative organisations. And they also to and fro had assistance by officers, two, three, four officers that were sometimes present and sometimes absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify. When you say that Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan were the second in command in their representative organisations, can you tell us the organisations that they were the second in command of, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes. To start with the Croat side, they had an organisation called HVO. The commander of this operational zone, Central Bosnia I think it was called, the commander was Colonel Blaskic. And Mr. Merdan was his second in command. And the BiH commander was Mr. Hadzihasanovic. He had his headquarters in the steel factory in Zenica. And Mr. Merdan was his second in command [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify, a few moments ago you said that Colonel Blaskic's second in command was Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes. No, Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic. So Blaskic's number 2 was Nakic.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Hadzihasanovic's second in command was Merdan?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether other than the representatives, various representatives, of the two parties, what other organisations were represented at the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: It differed from time to time. But we all -- almost always had representatives from the ICRC. Now and then, there were people from the UNHCR. And then now and then, local politicians were present. Sometimes police officers were present. And the meetings mostly took place in the municipality building in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, persons such as yourself, EC monitors, were also present.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes, of course. With interpreters and...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there ever any individuals from other western military organisations present at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. We also had almost all the time liaison officers from the UNPROFOR. And mainly, it was from the British Battalion in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, other than yourself, who were any other persons from the ECMM who may have occasionally attended the Busovaca Joint Commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zenica, there was a Danish monitor called Friis-Pedersen, something, who was the chairman of the commission. And after some two, three weeks, I was replacing him as a chairman of the committee. I had a German monitor called Schellschmidt, I think his name was, Dieter Schellschmidt. And I had later on a Dutch monitor, Henk Morsink. A Canadian monitor also took part now and then. Sorry, I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember some of the topics that were discussed at the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: It was a great variety of issues, but mostly it was problems with telecommunications, complaints about the broken lines. Sometimes it was water-supply problems. Of course, security problems. The Muslim part of the former Busovaca Municipality board, they had left or been forced out - I don't know which - out of Busovaca, and they had some kind of headquarters about 15 kilometres south of Busovaca in a place called Kacuni. And there -- sometimes we met with them, or sometimes we picked them up and took them into Busovaca to a meeting with the Croat part there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Busovaca Joint Commission during the time that you were present involved in any exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah, the commission as such was involved. But exchange or release, the word -- vocabulary changed now and then. But the members of the commission were, of course, involved in these negotiations and also the execution of decisions such as release of detainees or exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, do you recall the specifics of any of the prisoner exchanges that the commission was involved in, particularly in the first few weeks after you arrived in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: My first big business, so to say, was the prison in Kacuni - Kaonik, north of the centre of Busovaca. Kaonik prison was the name. When the -- starting this operation was -- the people from the Red Cross asked us if we knew where prisoner or detainees may be held in this area. And I remember, together with the German monitor Dieter Schellschmidt, we travelled around in Busovaca area and asked people "Do you know something about some prisoner camp" or something like that. And finally, we got information that there was such a camp in Kaonik. So we went there. And the guard denied us to -- he didn't let us in. And we asked who can give us permissions. And he advised us to contact the chief of police in Busovaca. So we went there and got permission to come in. And that was -- I have no idea how many people there was, but it was at least 20, 30, 40 people detained. And when we asked the commander there "Why are these men detained?" "He was a criminal." "Is he accused with something?" "No, not yet." Some of them were detained for murder, a large variety of reasons for persons being held there. And in one cell, we found I think it was seven young persons and I asked "Who are these? What's with these kind of people?" And if I remember correctly, the commanding officer there said they were criminals, and they were foreigners. And then I went into the cell and start talking to the youngsters there. And they explained to me in -- it was very large language problem, but I understood that some of them was from Libya and some from Egypt, some from Saudi Arabia, and some from Afghanistan. And I asked the commander again, "Why are you holding these people?" And then he explained that they had been found, as I understood, connecting to a car accident, and they had a lot of weapons and munitions in the car, and they also had a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, do you recall approximately how much money you were told that they had in their possession?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I was told it was 30 million US dollars. And I asked "Where are the suitcases with the money?" "I don't know," was the answer. And I asked him, "Have you seen it?" No, he hadn't seen it. "I heard it from this one who heard it from this one." It was, in my opinion, a kind of rumour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion about these -- or with these foreigners as to why they were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I asked the question: "Why are you here?" "What are you doing?" And they said "We are missionaries".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you interpret that to mean when they told you they were missionaries?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I had my opinion of what a missionary is, a person who is spreading some kind of religious belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what the person from the prison told you, that they had been arrested with weapons, did you ask them about weapons and why missionaries would need weapons?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I don't remember if I put that question. But to me it, seemed to be just as I said, much more of rumours than real proof of some criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, was the first time that you had seen any of these foreigners in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the last time you saw any such foreigners in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: In that situation, it was the only opportunity to see them. But I think when we saw, for instance, in the streets in Travnik in the beginning of June, I think it was not the Bosnian people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What makes you believe that these were not Bosnian people that you saw in early June in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: You had got some experiences during the months how Bosniak people were dressed and how they behaved. And these people we saw in Travnik, they were -- they didn't look like Bosniaks. Many of them wore a lot of big beards, and often they had green - what do you call it - scarves. And very mixed uniforms and heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the time that you saw these people -- let me rephrase. How many times in Travnik did you see such people?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I can't say a figure, but it was several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see such people that you might characterise as foreigners on other occasions in Bosnia; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Of course, it's hard to say because my memory is bad. It's 11 years ago. But if I say like this, among the colleagues of monitors, we had a common opinion that there existed such kind of peoples in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you base or what was this common opinion based on?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: It must be based on -- we saw them. And we heard people talking about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what these people were doing in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I have a very personal opinion. And I don't know if the Court is interested in hearing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could please tell us what your opinion is.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes. We had a very hard job to get to reunify the split municipalities. And as soon as we had succeeded in getting an agreement signed for a cease-fire or something like that, or freedom of movement, only the night after or some days after that it happens, things, like burning stable in the middle of the night; some person was killed by - how do you say it - anonymous people who moved around in the area. And in my opinion, it was some kind of people who did not wish to have the problems solved. They were carrying out -- what we heard, the word jihad. Bosnia jihad, the holy war in Bosnia. I don't know what kind of people who did this kind of actions, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, I'd like to take you back now to the persons that you told us were detained in Kaonik, the foreigners in Kaonik prison. Were these individuals ever the subject of discussions at the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Of course there were questions, perhaps more in general terms, of the detained people and to release the detainees, and also the term "prison of war" was used. And when we talked about prisoners of war, there were very often used the phrase "to exchange." But in the case of detainees, the phrase was used "to release" them. People who are held without legal support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any instances at the Busovaca Joint Commission where Mr. Merdan spoke about the need to have such foreign fighters released?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I don't know -- remember if it was in Busovaca Joint Commission, but at some meetings with the top personalities in Central Bosnia the question was raised. And there was also a proposal that all these Muslim detainees should be gathered in the prison in Zenica that was controlled by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- when you say "top personalities in Central Bosnia," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: On the military side, it was Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Hadzihasanovic. And they had political, if you call them, advisors or -- and also, of course, members of their military staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your experience with the senior leaders of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH including Mr. Hadzihasanovic and Mr. Merdan, did you gather the impression that they wanted the foreign fighters to be released from HVO control?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any idea or have any understanding as to why they wanted these foreign fighters released?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: No so to say written documents about that, but again, my personal opinion is that they were regarded as some kind of resources for the activities in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of activities, Mr. Junhov?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: There was a civil war going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall on approximately how many occasions you met with Mr. Merdan in the joint commissions or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: During my three months, I met him regularly, two, three, four times a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in total, approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Around 50 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on how many occasions did you meet with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: About a dozen times, 10 to 12. I met him in his office, and we met in our office. And I met him with some social activities. And I met with him on this, so to say, top-level meetings. I remember one such meeting in Kakanj, and one meeting also in -- I don't remember the name, north of Kiseljak. I don't remember the names. But I saw him 10 or 12 times during my visit there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, do you recall on any occasion whether General Hadzihasanovic discussed with you the release of the foreign fighters from Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: No, not he personally. But Mr. Merdan took up this question now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, do you recall any discussions where General Hadzihasanovic told you or perhaps hinted that efforts would be taken to free those individuals from Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, were you familiar with a subordinate unit of the 3rd Corps called the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you became aware of that unit.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. The first time was at an initial briefing in Zenica. We were presented with an organisation sheet of the 3rd Army Corps, BiH Army Corps, and there was in the normal military matter a square, 7th Operational Brigade I think it was called. And there was some asterisks and a footnote was "all-Muslim unit." And I recall that I made some reflection, BiH Army. Isn't that -- all of that army Muslim units? But obviously, by some reason this 7th Brigade was earmarked as some special unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who was in that unit or how that unit recruited soldiers?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I have no proof of it. But the common opinion within ECMM was that it was some kind of, say, French Foreign Legion, people recruited to this unit from abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the 7th Muslim Brigade? What type of role did it fulfil within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I think it's obvious by the name, operational unit, operational brigade. They operated in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they operate?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: In the area of Central Bosnia. Other units, they had very often three-figure names, 309th Brigade. They were local units, more or less like some kind of home guard or home defence forces. But the 7th Operational Brigade was operating in the whole area, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, did there come a time when any of these foreign fighters visited you in your office?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. That was -- I can't remember exactly the date of the event, but after some days of negotiations about releasing of detainees, some Croat officers were kidnapped. Some were in the Travnik-Vitez area, four or five officers, major -- captain/major level. And we got report of that. And then one or two days after that there appeared a person in the ECMM office. He was dressed with a turban, and he had a cotton plugged into the mouth so he talked very strange. And he handed over a videotape and explained that it was a message from the captured Croatian officers. So we took this videotape and drove by the car over to Vitez and handed it over to Colonel Blaskic's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, ever see that videotape?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I never saw the videotape, but I heard from officers in the Vitez staff that it was a message from these captured officers, and they prayed or -- to assist to release them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the individual who brought you this videotape on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. The same individual appeared some days later with a new tape. That was handled in the same way, so to say. We had no equipment in our office to see the tapes. We had no tape recorder or tape equipment. So in the same way, we handed it over to the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what if anything was done as a result of these videotapes?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah, there were new negotiations and discussions what to do with these. And of course, from the Muslim side, there was talk of exchange, to exchange, to release these HVO officers and detained Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, did an exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And again, I don't remember exactly the date. But I was some kind of spider in that net, and I had a command post in what we call the blue factory just out Busovaca. I think it was a factory that made some kind of wood equipment. And then we had spotted where the Muslim detainees were held and also where the Croat officers were held. And then we made a network with the assistance of the BritBat for communication reason and for transportation of the people. And then both sides had representatives on every place where the detainees existed. And in the blue factory in Busovaca, I had what I understood as some kind of commander of this Muslim force. And he got reports from his people out in the area, and finally the Muslim detainees were transported to the blue factory; and from there, they were loaded into BritBat's APCs and transported down to the coast, to Split, I think, for further travelling out of the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, sir, the Muslim detainees, were those local individuals or were those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: They must have been foreigners since they were transported out of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware at any time during the period you were in Central Bosnia of anything that took place in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Miletici. Could you help me to place it on the map, or...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I will ask the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 148.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Junhov, if you could please look at the second page, the names of the individuals who completed this report.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Erik Friis-Pedersen was the Danish, and he was my - should I say - predecessor of the Busovaca Joint Commission. And Allan Laustsen was Danish policeman and reserve officer of the Danish army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, does your name appear on this document?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And Mr. President, this is available on Sanction if people would like to view it on their screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 2 C of this document.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: "The Croat village Miletici. Five inhabitants were murdered by shots and knives yesterday. They were all men, aged between approximately 20 and 60."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, having seen this document, does that refresh your memory as to the events in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. It was, again, some rumours that made Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic interested in going to this place. And Friis-Pedersen was together with them, and I think they were transported there by BritBat, or if they drove up there by the ECMM vehicle I don't know. But they found a small village high up in the -- if I remember correctly, high up in the Bila valley where -- this is written by Friis-Pedersen, of course, because he was the monitor who was there. These people were killed, and according to witnesses, as Arab-speaking men dressed in ordinary uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just interrupt you, because actually what I'd like to talk to you about is that relationship between Mr. Merdan and Mr. Nakic. According to the document you have before you, Prosecution Exhibit 148, Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan went with Mr. Friis-Pedersen to the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of the fact that these two individuals, Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan, were from what might be characterised as warring parties --

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- can you explain to us a little bit about why the two of them would go together to visit this village?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I think they were, both of them, driven by some wish to get facts. They were members of the Busovaca Joint Commission, or in this case, joint operational centre in Vitez. And they heard rumours something had happened up there. And they say, "okay, let's go there and find out what has happened."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you characterise the relationship between these two men based on your attending numerous meetings of the Busovaca Joint Commission with them. How did they get along together? How did they interact? These types of things.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Let's say it was not a very friendly attitude, but it was some kind of professional, cooperative attitude. They had a wish or a will to find facts and to solve problems. And they realised, of course, that they had to do it together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other instances where the two of them, perhaps with an ECMM monitor, went to other places where there were rumours or allegations of crimes being committed?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah. I was together with these two officers in a small village. I think it's called Ostici, south of Busovaca, that had been -- there were no living people left there. And it was a Muslim village. And I noticed in the refugee -- the ICRC camp in Busovaca they had registered people from this village who were refugees. And we went there to investigate what and found out what happened in that village. I think you have a similar report on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That document, sir, can now be returned. Madam Usher can retrieve that. Let me ask you a few questions about Mr. Merdan. Based on again, the numerous times you met with him, can you tell us a little bit about Mr. Merdan as a military man, as a deputy commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I found him professional, and he was in my opinion quite a balanced person. I never saw him - what do you say - in effect or that he lost his temper. And he always listened carefully what we said. He was a professional officer, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or based on what you observed or saw, did you come to any conclusions about what his specific role was in the 3rd Corps, what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah, I have, of course - again it's a personal opinion; I can't prove it by some written documents - but as he was so often together with us, as Mr. Nakic was out in the area controlled by the other part, of course when he came back to his office, he reported what he had seen and learned. So he was some kind of -- I think in my written statement, I have quoted a "legal spy", I think I used the expression. But of course, his job was to contribute to these local commissions could work, and he was authorised by his commanders, of course, to take part in this job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, do you also remember in your written statement indicating that Mr. Merdan was the "eyes and the ears for the commander, General Hadzihasanovic"?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah, that's why I said he was a legal spy. But don't misinterpret this expression "legal spy." It's quoted in my written. He had -- that was his job, to cooperate with us and with the UNPROFOR and other organisations in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the type of commander General Hadzihasanovic was, again, based on the 10 to 12 times that you met with him at various places during the time period you were in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: It's almost the same impression that I got from Mr. Merdan. Hadzihasanovic was -- in my view, he was a professional officer. He was, could you say, polite or -- I went several times to his staff to complain about observations we had made. And sometimes I met with him personally or sometimes with some of his staff members. And it was no problem to get in contact, and we discussed the problem. I also met him, as I mentioned before, a couple of times in social activities. There was a choir concert when he invited us personally to go there. And we also were invited to some kind of party. And of course, he behaved like a civilised officer. And no problems to discuss whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the sense or the impression from your meetings with him that he was fully informed as to the situation on the ground? And did he seem to you to be prepared to discuss issues when you had meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Not always. During the weeks before the Guca Gora, there were fightings going on up in the area. And when I was denied by Muslim people at the checkpoint outside Zenica, I was denied to go into the area to see what's going on, so I went down to the army corps staff and complained about that. And I got an escort from the army corps staff by some military police. And again, when we tried to enter the area, we run into a road blockation with, as I understood - what do you call them - Muslim foreigners or soldiers fired in the air and didn't allow us to go into the area. And then I went back again to the army corps staff and complained about that. And then I got the answer "unit's out of control."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on any other occasion discuss with General Hadzihasanovic the foreign fighters that you believed were in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Not person to person, but in the army corps staff and in the joint commission meetings there were such kind of discussions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response of the 3rd Corps representatives when this subject matter was discussed at these joint commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: They never denied the existence of it, but very often declared that there were units operating on their own hands and out of control of the command, commanding organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall which unit or units they were referring to when they indicated that these units were not in their hands or out of control?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Normally, people understood that when these type of actions were taken, it was understood that it was people belonging to the 7th Brigade. But, of course, I did not have possibilities to identify the individual soldiers or men, the military insignias also. So I have no juridical proof that it was. But every people that we met with and talked to said, "Oh, it's the 7th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what your thoughts about that were at the time, that this 7th Muslim Brigade was not under the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall thinking about the fact that the 7th Muslim Brigade was not under the 3rd Corps command? What did you think about that when you were told?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: My immediate reflection was "obviously there exists a unit that is operating in the area." That was out of question. "And who is commanding them?" That's the problem. The person who is responsible for the area is the commander of the 3rd Army Corps. And this unit was operating in his area and also, of course, in the area controlled by the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the response that you gave in your written statement to the investigators about the 7th Muslim Brigade and their role within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Could you read it for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you two or three sentences and see if this triggers any recollections in your mind. You say "I was under the impression that the Mujahedin belonged to the 7th Muslim Brigade, but Merdan also stated that the 7th Muslim Brigade was out of control. In my opinion, it is strange to claim that the only mobile unit within the 3rd Corps could be out of control. 7th Muslim Brigade was the elite unit, and obviously the most important unit of the 3rd Corps." Do you remember saying that to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can I ask you, other than what you said here, if you have any independent recollections as to what you thought when you were told these kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: As I remember it, it was some kind of established opinion that the 7th Muslim Brigade had some kind of special standing in the organisation, or if we say they had -- if we call it more freedom of movement in the area or... They seemed to me to operate more or less on their hand. Or if they had some orders from the army corps I don't know because I never seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you've told us they seemed to move throughout the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a few final questions. I would like to ask you about any destruction that you personally witnessed during the time you were in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: If you don't -- if you accept the dating might fail, but the mosque in Ahmici, I think it was the 9th of April or something like that. That was one of these grave events conducted by HVO special forces. And then I saw a number of churches primarily in the Travnik area, Catholic church, an old church in the central Travnik close to the marketplace. I went there because I had heard from someone that they had an interpreter that might be willing to assist us. So I went there to ask for this man, and then a female officer in the parish living close to the church asked me if she could show me inside the church. So, of course, so I joined her and found much of the inventories in the church were destroyed. Sculpture of the saints were decaptured [sic], paintings were cut in pieces, furnitures were broken, windows blown out. To me, total meaningless destruction of holy things, holy... And there was another church, I don't remember the name, just east of Travnik. It seemed to have been some kind of monastery or perhaps a school because a lot of books were thrown out of the windows. The inventory was broken. And this church was also shelled, hit by mortars, grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could interrupt you for just a moment. I'd like to return to the church you were telling us about in Travnik with the damage that you described. Do you know which church that was?

utterances.speaker: TORBJORN JUNHOV
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a Catholic church. I don't know if there were more than one Catholic church in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
